idiom_name: class (reference semantics) with a private constructor; never a record, never a struct
implementation_notes: C# classes are reference types: assignment copies the reference, never the object, and the compiler generates no copy constructor - so the mixin's job is already done by modelling an identity-bearing type as a class instead of a struct, which is the decision to state explicitly (connection, credential, session, transaction). Keep the constructor private and construct through a factory, mark the class `sealed` so no subclass can reintroduce copying, and never add the `record` modifier: `record class` synthesises a protected copy constructor plus the `with` expression, which is exactly the duplication path this pattern forbids. Structs, by contrast, copy on assignment, argument passing and boxing, and C# offers no way to suppress those copies, so a type that must not be copied must not be a struct. The classic base-class form survives for the inverse problem - a value type that must stay usable as a value but must refuse ICloneable-style duplication.
pitfalls: `record class` (and `record struct`) silently adds a copy constructor, value equality and `with`; the modifier on an identity type reintroduces precisely the copying this pattern removes.
A struct cannot be made non-copyable - assignment, boxing and `in`-parameter copies all duplicate the fields - so an identity-bearing type must be a class, and the class-ness is part of the contract.
`MemberwiseClone()` is protected on Object and returns a shallow copy; a subclass (or the type itself while prototyping) can turn it into a usable clone, which is why `sealed` matters.

Serialisers and ORMs reconstruct instances through reflection (for example uninitialised-object APIs), so compile-time non-copyability does not stop a deserialiser from materialising a second instance.
